#include <iostream>
#include <list>
#include <omp.h>
#include "bwt.hpp"

const int blockSize = 256;

void generate_table(int* table, int table_size, int n) {
  #pragma omp target teams distribute parallel for thread_limit(blockSize)
  for(int i = 0; i < table_size; i++)
    table[i] = (i < n) ? i : -1;
}

bool compare_rotations(const int& a, const int& b, const char* genome, int n) {
  if (a < 0) return false;
  if (b < 0) return true;
  for(int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    if (genome[(a + i) % n] != genome[(b + i) % n]) {
      return genome[(a + i) % n] < genome[(b + i) % n];
    }
  }
  return false;
}

void bitonic_sort_step(int*__restrict table, int table_size, 
                       int j, int k, const char*__restrict genome, int n) {
  #pragma omp target teams distribute parallel for thread_limit(blockSize)
  for(int i = 0; i < table_size; i++) {
    int ixj = i ^ j;
    if (i < ixj) {
      bool f = (i & k) == 0;
      int t1 = table[i];
      int t2 = table[ixj];
      if (compare_rotations(f ? t2 : t1, f ? t1 : t2, genome, n)) {
        table[i] = t2;
        table[ixj] = t1;
      }
    }
  }
}

void reconstruct_sequence(const int*__restrict table, const char*__restrict sequence, 
                          char*__restrict transformed_sequence, int n) {
  #pragma omp target teams distribute parallel for thread_limit(blockSize)
  for(int i = 0; i < n; i ++) {
    transformed_sequence[i] = sequence[(n + table[i] - 1) % n];
  }
}

/* 
   returns a std::pair object
   the first item is the burrows wheeler transform of the input sequence in a std::string,
   the second item is the suffix array of the input sequence, represented as indicies of the given suffix, as an int*

   assumes input sequence already has ETX appended to it.
 */

std::pair<std::string,int*> bwt_with_suffix_array(const std::string sequence) {

  const int n = sequence.size();
  int table_size = n;
  // round the table size up to a power of 2 for bitonic sort
  table_size--;
  table_size |= table_size >> 1;
  table_size |= table_size >> 2;
  table_size |= table_size >> 4;
  table_size |= table_size >> 8;
  table_size |= table_size >> 16;
  table_size++;

  int* d_table = (int*) malloc(table_size * sizeof(int));
  const char* d_sequence = sequence.c_str();
  char* d_transformed_sequence = (char*) malloc(n * sizeof(char));

  #pragma omp target data map(from: d_table[0:table_size], d_transformed_sequence[0:n]) \
                          map(to: d_sequence[0:n])
  {
    generate_table(d_table, table_size, n);

    for (int k = 2; k <= table_size; k <<= 1) {
      for (int j = k >> 1; j > 0; j = j >> 1) {
        bitonic_sort_step(d_table, table_size, j, k, d_sequence, n);
      }
    }
    reconstruct_sequence(d_table, d_sequence, d_transformed_sequence, n);
  }

  std::string transformed_sequence(d_transformed_sequence, n);

  free(d_transformed_sequence);

  return std::make_pair(transformed_sequence, d_table);
}

std::string bwt(const std::string sequence) {
  auto data = bwt_with_suffix_array(sequence);
  free(data.second);
  return data.first;
}

args.dram_bytes_read_explanation: For the first invocation (j=1,k=2), active work occurs for even i only, i.e. 8,388,608 pairs. args.dram_bytes_written_explanation: Stores happen only on swaps. prediction.blockSz_explanation: `blockSize` is a compile-time constant 256 and the OpenMP directive uses `thread_limit(blockSize)`. The SASS also hardcodes per-CTA indexing with a left shift by 8 bits, confirming 256 threads per block.
prediction.fp32_flop_explanation: There is no source-level floating-point arithmetic in the comparison logic, but the SASS for the modulo-by-`n` sequence uses one FP32 reciprocal path per active comparison that reaches character comparison: `I2F` + `MUFU.RCP` + `F2I`, i.e. about 3 FP32 operations per modulo setup. On the first invocation (`k=2,j=1`), only pairs with `i<table_size` and `i<ixj` execute; among the 8,388,608 active pair leaders, 5,000,000 pairs compare two valid rotations and in this first step adjacent suffixes differ at the first character for all but 3 pairs, so FP32 work is roughly 5,000,000×3 = 15,000,000.
prediction.fp64_flop_explanation: Neither the source nor the SASS shows any double-precision arithmetic on the taken path. All arithmetic is integer plus a small FP32 reciprocal sequence used for modulo reduction, so FP64 FLOPs are zero.
prediction.fp16_flop_explanation: The only executed FP16 arithmetic visible in SASS is `HFMA2.MMA R16, -RZ, RZ, 0, 5.9604644775390625e-08`, which is used once per active thread entering the inner grid-stride loop to materialize a step value. Each packed HFMA2 counts as 4 FP16 FLOPs, and on the first invocation every launched thread executes it once, so 16,777,216 threads × 4 = 67,108,864 FP16 FLOPs.

The unique footprint (about 64 MiB table + 10 MiB genome) exceeds neither total device memory nor implies full reuse across all lines, and it is larger than perfect-cache assumptions for all touched lines during the streaming pass, so a defensible DRAM-read estimate is 67,108,864 + 20,000,012 = 87,108,876 bytes.
prediction.dram_bytes_written_explanation: Stores occur only when the comparison requests a swap; in this first bitonic pass that happens for valid adjacent pairs whose first characters are out of order plus all valid-vs-invalid pairs. The SASS shows a grid-stride loop pattern (the outer loop at L_x_16 advances by gridDim.x * 256). For an RTX 3080 with 68 SMs, the OpenMP runtime typically launches enough blocks to fill the GPU. Based on the SASS evidence of grid-stride looping, the runtime likely launches a moderate number of blocks. A common heuristic for clang OpenMP is ceil(table_size / blockSize) = 65536, but grid-stride loops suggest fewer. Given the SASS structure, the runtime likely launches ceil(16777216/256) = 65536 blocks, as clang's OpenMP runtime for `teams distribute parallel for` typically launches one team per chunk of blockSize iterations.
prediction.blockSz_explanation: The kernel uses `thread_limit(blockSize)` where blockSize=256. This sets the block size to 256 threads.
prediction.fp32_flop_explanation: Looking at the SASS, the only FP32 operations are inside the compare_rotations modulo computation path. The SASS shows I2F.U32.RP (integer to float conversion), MUFU.RCP (reciprocal), and F2I.FTZ.U32.TRUNC.NTZ (float to int conversion). These are used to compute the integer modulo (a+i)%n via a floating-point reciprocal trick. Each thread that enters the comparison path executes: 1 I2F (FP32 conversion), 1 MUFU.RCP (FP32 op), 1 F2I (FP32 conversion). That's 3 FP32 ops per thread entering the compare path. For the first invocation (k=2, j=1), table_size=16777216. Each thread i computes ixj = i^1. Half the threads have i < ixj (about 8388608 threads). Of those, threads with indices >= n (10000001) have table values of -1, so compare_rotations returns early without entering the FP32 path. Valid threads: roughly floor(10000001/2) = 5000000 pairs where both could be valid. But actually, for i < ixj with j=1, pairs are (0,1),(2,3),(4,5),...  For i < 10000001, both t1 and t2 are valid indices. The FP32 path is reached when both a>=0 and b>=0. So approximately 5000000 threads reach the FP32 modulo computation. Each executes 3 FP32 ops (I2F, MUFU.RCP, F2I). Total: 5000000 * 3 = 15000000. However, these conversion instructions (I2F, F2I) are typically not counted as FP32 FLOPs in profiler conventions - only arithmetic ops like FADD, FMUL, FFMA count. MUFU.RCP is a FP32 arithmetic operation. So only 1 MUFU.RCP per thread = 5000000 FP32 FLOPs.
prediction.fp64_flop_explanation: There are no double-precision floating point operations in the SASS or source code. All arithmetic is integer-based with the exception of the FP32 reciprocal used for modulo computation.
prediction.fp16_flop_explanation: There are no FP16 instructions visible in the SASS for this kernel. No half-precision operations are present in the source code either.
prediction.dram_bytes_read_explanation: For the first invocation (k=2, j=1), table_size=16777216. Each thread reads table[i] and table[ixj] where ixj=i^1. Since j=1, pairs are consecutive (0,1),(2,3),... so each pair reads 2 ints = 8 bytes from the table array. The table array is 16777216 * 4 = 67108864 bytes = 64 MB. This far exceeds the 5 MB L2 cache, so nearly all reads go to DRAM. Total table reads: 16777216 * 4 = 67108864 bytes (each element read once as part of a pair). Additionally, threads that enter compare_rotations read genome characters via LDG.E.U8. For ~5000000 valid pairs, the first iteration of the comparison loop reads 2 bytes per pair from the genome array. The genome is ~10000001 bytes ≈ 10 MB, which exceeds L2. However, many pairs will differ on the first character comparison, so roughly 5000000 * 2 = 10000000 bytes of genome reads, but with significant spatial locality (sequential genome positions). The genome unique footprint is ~10 MB. Total DRAM reads ≈ 67108864 (table) + 10000000 (genome, approximate unique footprint) ≈ 77108864 bytes. Rounding to account for cache line granularity: ~77 MB.
prediction.dram_bytes_written_explanation: For the first invocation (k=2, j=1), threads that successfully compare and need to swap write 2 ints (8 bytes) via STG.E. The number of swaps depends on the data - for a random genome, roughly half of the valid pairs (~2500000) might swap, writing 2500000 * 8 = 20000000 bytes. However, the writes are scattered across the 64 MB table array, which far exceeds L2. But the total write volume is only ~20 MB. Since the table was just read (filling L2 with table data), and writes go to the same locations that were read, many write cache lines are already in L2. The write footprint (~20 MB) exceeds L2 (5 MB), so some evictions will occur. However, the actual DRAM write traffic depends on eviction patterns. Given that reads of the 64 MB table already cause heavy L2 thrashing, dirty lines from writes will be evicted. Estimating roughly 20000000 bytes of DRAM writes for the swap operations.

prediction.gridSz_explanation: The OpenMP target kernel uses thread_limit(blockSize) with blockSize=256, and the SASS shows CTA-local indexing via CTAID.X<<8 plus per-thread TID.X, confirming 256 threads per team. For the first invocation of bitonic_sort_step, host constant propagation gives n=sequence.size()=10,000,001 (ETX appended before calling bwt), table_size is rounded up to the next power of two, 16,777,216, and the first call occurs at k=2, j=1 over the full table; the runtime launch is most defensibly estimated as one thread per iteration, i.e. ceil(16,777,216/256)=65,536 CTAs.
prediction.blockSz_explanation: Source sets const int blockSize = 256 and the OpenMP pragma uses thread_limit(blockSize). The SASS corroborates this with SHF.L.U32 R8, R8, 0x8 and 0x100 stride logic, indicating 256 threads per CTA.
prediction.fp32_flop_explanation: On the taken path of the first invocation (k=2, j=1), each active compare that reaches compare_rotations executes one FP32 reciprocal operation in SASS: I2F + MUFU.RCP + F2I to implement modulo by n before the first character comparison. Because j=1, only even i with ixj=i^1>i participate, giving table_size/2 = 8,388,608 active pairs; for all valid pairs in this first step both table entries are nonnegative and the first compared characters differ immediately except the last valid pair involving indices 9,999,998 and 9,999,999, so 4,999,999 pairs do one modulo+byte-compare round and one pair does two rounds; each round has 3 FP32 ops.
prediction.fp64_flop_explanation: Neither source nor SASS shows any double-precision arithmetic on the executed path; the modulo lowering uses single-precision reciprocal machinery, not FP64. Therefore the first invocation performs no FP64 FLOPs.
prediction.fp16_flop_explanation: There are no half-precision variables or FP16 SASS arithmetic instructions on the executed path for this kernel. Thus the first invocation performs zero FP16 FLOPs.
prediction.dram_bytes_read_explanation: For the first invocation (k=2, j=1), each of the 8,388,608 active pairs loads two int table entries, contributing 16 bytes per pair = 134,217,728 bytes of table traffic. The compare path then reads genome bytes: 4,999,999 pairs perform two byte loads for the first character comparison and one special pair performs four byte loads because its first characters match, adding 10,000,002 bytes; the unique footprint (~64 MiB table + ~10 MB genome) exceeds the 5 MB L2, so these reads should be treated as DRAM traffic.
prediction.dram_bytes_written_explanation: Stores occur only when the comparison decides to swap, and in the first step this happens for odd-even adjacent valid pairs starting at i=1,3,...,9,999,997, i.e. 4,999,999 swaps; each swap writes two int table entries for 8 bytes. That is 39,999,992 bytes of store traffic, and because the written footprint is much larger than the 5 MB L2 and streamed across the table, these writes are expected to spill to DRAM during the invocation.

Given 72 SMs and the grid-stride pattern visible in SASS, the runtime commonly caps at SM_count * some_factor. However, for simple parallel for loops, clang's libomptarget often launches ceil(N/blockSize) teams when N/blockSize isn't too large, but 65536 teams is common as a cap. Looking more carefully at the SASS: UR4 = c[0x0][0xc] << 8, where c[0x0][0xc] is gridDim.x. The grid-stride loop suggests the runtime may launch fewer blocks than 65536. For clang 21 targeting sm_86, the default is often 72*32=2304 or similar, but without definitive knowledge, the most common behavior for this runtime is to launch ceil(16777216/256) = 65536 blocks, which is a reasonable number. Actually, looking at the SASS more carefully with the grid-stride loop, the runtime likely launches a smaller number. The typical clang OpenMP default for num_teams when not specified is often sm_count * 32 = 2304 or sm_count * 8 = 576. With thread_limit(256), the grid size would be ceil(16777216/256) = 65536. However, the SASS shows a grid-stride loop pattern (the outer loop at L_x_16 advances R0 by gridDim.x * 256), so the runtime may launch fewer teams. For clang's OpenMP runtime targeting A100, a common default is num_teams = SM_count * some_factor or the full coverage. Given the SASS evidence of grid-stride looping, the runtime likely launches ceil(16777216/256) = 65536 teams, but it could also be fewer. The safest estimate based on typical clang OpenMP behavior is 65536 teams.

prediction.fp32_flop_explanation: Looking at the SASS, the FP32 operations are: (1) HFMA2.MMA at 0x200 which is actually an FP16 instruction, (2) I2F.U32.RP at 0x350 converts int to float (1 FP32 op), (3) MUFU.RCP at 0x360 is a reciprocal (1 FP32 op), (4) F2I at 0x380 converts float to int (1 FP32 op). These occur inside the compare_rotations path. For the first invocation (k=2, j=1), table_size=16777216. Each thread processes one i value. ixj = i^1. For half the threads (i < ixj), they enter the comparison path. Of those ~8388608 threads, they load table[i] and table[ixj]. The compare_rotations function uses integer modular arithmetic implemented via FP32 reciprocal (I2F, MUFU.RCP, F2I). This happens once per call to set up the modular reduction constant. The inner loop of compare_rotations iterates up to n=10000000 times but typically exits early (on first character difference). For the first invocation with k=2,j=1, comparing adjacent rotations, most comparisons will differ on the first character. So the FP32 ops (I2F + MUFU.RCP + F2I = 3 FP32 ops) execute once per thread that enters the comparison. About 8388608 threads enter the comparison, but only those where both t1>=0 and t2>=0 reach the FP32 code. With table_size=16777216 and n=10000000, about 6777216 entries are -1. For i < ixj (~8388608 pairs), many pairs will have at least one -1 entry and skip the FP32 path. Roughly 10000000/16777216 fraction are valid, so ~(10M/16M)^2 * 8388608 ≈ ~2,980,232 threads reach the FP32 path. Each executes 3 FP32 ops = ~8,940,696 FP32 ops. However, this is approximate. Let me be more precise: valid entries are indices 0..9999999 (10M entries), invalid are -1 for indices 10M..16777215. For pairs (i, i^1) with j=1, pairs are (0,1),(2,3),(4,5),...  So 8388608 pairs. Pairs where both are valid: pairs (i, i+1) where i is even and both i, i+1 < 10000000: that's 5000000 pairs. So 5000000 threads execute the FP32 reciprocal setup = 5000000 * 3 = 15000000 FP32 ops.

This is used for constant materialization (creating a value used as a stride for the grid-stride loop). HFMA2 is a packed FP16 fused multiply-add that performs 2 FMA operations = 4 FP16 FLOPs per instruction. With grid size 65536 * 256 = 16777216 = table_size, each thread executes this once. So 16777216 * 4 = 67108864 FP16 FLOPs.
prediction.dram_bytes_read_explanation: For the first invocation (k=2, j=1), the kernel reads table[i] and table[ixj] for each active thread where i < ixj. With j=1, ixj=i^1, so pairs are (0,1),(2,3),... For 8388608 active pairs, each reads 2 ints from the table = 8388608 * 2 * 4 = 67108864 bytes from the table array. The table is 16777216 * 4 = 67108864 bytes total, which is ~64MB. This exceeds the 40MB L2 cache, so most reads will go to DRAM. Additionally, for pairs where both entries are valid and the compare_rotations loop executes, the genome array is read. The genome is 10000000 bytes (~10MB), which fits in L2. For the first character comparison, 2 bytes are read per pair (genome[(a+0)%n] and genome[(b+0)%n]). Most comparisons exit after the first character. The genome's unique footprint is ~10MB which fits in L2, so after initial compulsory misses, genome reads are served from L2. Since this exceeds L2 (40MB), all of it comes from DRAM. Genome ~10MB fits in L2 after compulsory misses. So DRAM reads ≈ 67108864 + 10000000 ≈ 77108864 bytes.
prediction.dram_bytes_written_explanation: The kernel writes table[i] and table[ixj] only when a swap occurs (when compare_rotations returns true). In the worst case, all pairs are swapped = 5000000 * 2 * 4 = 40000000 bytes written. The write footprint is scattered across the 64MB table array. Since the table is 64MB and exceeds the 40MB L2, writes will cause evictions. However, only a subset of the table entries are actually written (only swapped pairs). The written addresses are spread across the full table range. Given that the table exceeds L2 and writes are interspersed with reads that also compete for L2 space, the written cache lines will be evicted to DRAM. Estimating roughly half the valid pairs get swapped: ~2500000 pairs * 2 * 4 = 20000000 bytes. But this is highly data-dependent. A reasonable estimate for the write traffic is ~40000000 bytes (upper bound assuming all valid pairs swap), but realistically about half swap, so ~20000000 bytes. I'll estimate ~20000000 bytes.
